> Last updated: October 21, 2026 20:30 UTC

In the early morning of October 21, LiteLLM's release pipeline was compromised and pushed v1.107.0 to the docker registry and PyPi. This version contained compiled malware which steals credentials and loads remote-code execution tools. All previous versions are safe, and the impacted releases have been pulled. Enterprise Customers running the private enterprise release of LiteLLM were not impacted.

Update (20:30 UTC): We believe we have identified the attack chain which facilitated this attack. The attacker had to compromise multiple independent security controls to be successful. See How this happened below.

## TLDR; ​

- A malicious litellm==1.107.0 package was published to PyPI and was live for approximately 2 hours (11:39 UTC to 13:23 UTC). It has since been pulled.

- Docker images v1.107.0 , latest , main-latest , and main-stable were compromised from 11:46 UTC to 14:20 UTC. The v1.107.0 image was removed, and the others were pointed at secure sources.

- Enterprise Customers running the private enterprise release of LiteLLM were not impacted.

## Overview ​

At 4:00 AM PST October 21, LiteLLM's release pipeline was compromised and pushed v1.107.0 to the docker registry and PyPi. This version contained compiled malware which steals credentials and loads remote-code execution tools. All previous versions are safe, and the impacted releases have been pulled.

## Confirmed Affected Versions ​

The following LiteLLM artifacts were impacted:

- PyPI: litellm==1.107.0 : all seven wheels, live from 11:39:51 to 13:23 UTC

- Docker Hub: v1.107.0 , latest , main-latest , and main-stable : pointed to compromised image index sha256:1bbcb1443bc962e45f5aad53fe3d2c30600e0379715fb6c664cdd3ac126c339e from 11:46:56 to 14:20 UTC

- GHCR: v1.107.0 , latest , main-latest , and main-stable : pointed to the compromised image indexes below from 11:46:56 UTC until they were made unavailable by 13:51 UTC ghcr.io/berriai/litellm : sha256:1bbcb1443bc9… ghcr.io/berriai/litellm-database : sha256:c00f9d92c427… ghcr.io/berriai/litellm-non_root : sha256:7b00e91cd2fe…

- ghcr.io/berriai/litellm : sha256:1bbcb1443bc9…

- ghcr.io/berriai/litellm-database : sha256:c00f9d92c427…

- ghcr.io/berriai/litellm-non_root : sha256:7b00e91cd2fe…

The official v1.107.0 source tag in GitHub does not contain the malicious files. The compromised artifacts were built from an attacker-controlled repository.

If you installed or ran any of these artifacts, review the recommendations below immediately.

Note: These artifacts have already been removed from PyPI, Docker Hub, and GHCR.

## Who is affected ​

You are affected if you used an unpinned version of LiteLLM between 11:39 and 13:23 UTC via pip or if you used the docker image v1.107.0 , latest , main-latest , or main-stable between 11:46 and 14:20 UTC.

OSS Users

If you ran pip install on LiteLLM v1.107.0 or started the docker image in the compromised interval, assume it is compromised.

For the time being, please pin your version to 1.106.2 or any explicit version published prior to now.

Enterprise Customers

There currently exists a private LiteLLM registry for enterprise customers, in which we are distributing an embargoed release that remediates a vulnerability whose disclosure date is scheduled for October 27. Our private registry is not affected. If you are an enterprise customer pulling from our private registry you are not affected.

### How to check if you are affected ​

- If an environment started Python with litellm==1.107.0, treat that environment as compromised. You can check with pip show litellm .

- If a container executed affected image digest sha256:1bbcb1443bc962e45f5aad53fe3d2c30600e0379715fb6c664cdd3ac126c339e, treat it as compromised.

- Search filesystem evidence for litellm-1.107.0.dist-info, cook.pth, and sitecustomize.py. Finding one confirms exposure, but not finding one does not prove the environment is clean.

We will be posting more detail on how specifically to find indication of compromise. For now, you can find details of the attack and our initial responses in this GitHub Issue .

### What to do if you are affected ​

These instructions are courtesy of LidorMachluf , who helped us to detect this incident.

Don't start with pip install . Any Python start in the affected environment runs cook.pth and sitecustomize.py again, and that includes running pip.

- From the shell, delete cook.pth , cook.py , sitecustomize.py and any matching __pycache__/cook*.pyc and sitecustomize*.pyc from every affected site-packages.

- Kill the detached python daemon (it holds /tmp/remote_code_loader.lock ).

- Reinstall pinned to litellm==1.106.2 . Rebuilding images and venvs from scratch is better.

- If 1.107.0 was ever installed on a host with outbound internet, assume the exfil succeeded. If the marker file exists, the exfil is confirmed. If it doesn't, that proves nothing: containers and tmp cleanup remove it.

- Rotate everything listed above that the host could reach. In particular: the instance/task IAM role every provider key stored in the LiteLLM proxy DB , plus the master and virtual keys the DATABASE_URL password any secret that was in the environment of any process on the host

- the instance/task IAM role

- every provider key stored in the LiteLLM proxy DB , plus the master and virtual keys

- the DATABASE_URL password

- any secret that was in the environment of any process on the host

- Check CloudTrail for GetCallerIdentity from the instance role around install time, then for use of the role's credentials from outside your infrastructure.

## How this happened? ​

After the prior incident in March, we meaningfully hardened our CI release pipeline . We moved releases to a private repo, have a strict set of workflows used in order to create them via Trusted GitHub Publishers, made our docker release tags immutable, and are signing docker images.

### Normal release flow ​

- Cut a release-candidate branch and tag. This happens on Friday at 3AM, and the branch and tag do not change.

- Qualify the release candidate. We run the code through our integration tests, both publicly through CircleCI and privately through Buildkite, and check that everything is correct.

- Create artifacts. This step is a GitHub workflow that runs in a private repo, and creates artifacts based on the SHA that has been qualified. This must be done by an engineer with write permissions to the private release repo.

- Deploy artifacts to testing environment. We run a second round of testing against the produced artifacts.

- Publish the artifacts. This is a GitHub workflow that uses Trusted GitHub Publishers to publish the artifacts made in the previous step. Publishing can only be performed by an account locked to a specific laptop physically located within our office at all times. No docker image is rebuilt at publish time.

### How it was undermined ​

- On Monday, we temporarily expanded release permissions to allow two internal engineers to publish daily bugfix backports for customers.

- The attacker had access to three sets of developer GitHub CLI credentials ( more on this below ). One of these had the ability to run GitHub workflows.

- The attacker tried to merge a change to allow the releaser to be pointed at a different source repository, but was unable to due to our protections. One of the tokens held by the attacker belonged to one of our two GitHub organization owners. The attacker used this to disable branch protections and force push the change.

- Finally, they ran the compromised workflow, pointed at a lookalike repository ( Berri-AI/litellm instead of BerriAI/litellm ), which signed and published the poisoned artifacts.

### GitHub CLI OAuth token exposure ​

After a thorough investigation, we have observed specific situations in which Claude Code will embed a user's GitHub CLI OAuth token into a response body, and in situations where response bodies are logged, these tokens may appear in LiteLLM logs.

### Access to our internal LiteLLM deployment ​

We identified an unexpected, innocuously named user account in our internal LiteLLM deployment, which was exposed to the public internet. We believe the attacker gained access to this deployment, obtained the GitHub CLI OAuth tokens from its logs, and subsequently used those credentials to compromise our release workflow.

We have not yet confirmed how the attacker gained access to our internal deployment, but currently suspect it was through a recently patched vulnerability.

### Continued investigation ​

We are still working on confirming some of the above, and identifying a timeline. We will post additional details as we discover them.

## Response and Remediation ​

We have already taken the following steps:

- Removed compromised packages from PyPI

- Revoked maintainer credentials to minimal necessary while we investigate the scope of compromise

If you discover a security issue in LiteLLM, please report it through our bug bounty program .

On October 21, our release pipeline published a compromised litellm==1.107.0 to PyPI and to our container registries. The incident post covers the affected artifacts and what to do if you ran them. We have completed our investigation into the actions taken by the threat actor, and can confidently assert the timeline and sequence of events that led to the publication of the malicious v1.107.0 release.

We posted regular status updates during our investigation yesterday reflecting the scenario to the best of our knowledge as the investigation proceeded. The investigation was ongoing, and some assumptions and beliefs in those updates were later proven to be inaccurate or incomplete. This post is the canonical source of truth.

## Narrative ​

On May 27, 2026, a configuration file was committed to the public LiteLLM-Labs/lite-harness repository which inadvertently contained the master key to a deployment of the LiteLLM Agent Platform, an open source tool we use for orchestrating agents. The error was quickly identified, the commit force-pushed over, and we identified the exposed keys as requiring revocation. However, key revocation did not occur for the master key.

### GitHub Owner Access ​

LiteLLM Agent Platform was an experimental project for self-hosted cloud agents to file PRs to GitHub repositories. In order to create PRs, the system was configured with a GitHub authentication token. The token in question was not associated with a service account and was not scoped down. The key used was a GitHub CLI OAuth token associated with our GitHub organization owner's account.

On October 10th, the threat actor used this key to gain access to our LiteLLM Agent Platform and extracted this GitHub CLI OAuth token. From this point onwards, the threat actor had owner-level access to all repositories in our GitHub. GitHub CLI tokens are post-2fa and not subject to GitHub's "super-user" 2fa reauth flows associated with sensitive organization or repository actions.

### Exfiltrating additional tokens ​

Using the access provided by the Github CLI OAuth token, the threat actor began to perform additional credential exfiltration actions. They authored commits into branches on internal repositories to execute workflows designed to exfiltrate any tokens and secrets configured to be available to CI in our repositories. In so doing, they acquired similar GitHub CLI Oauth tokens associated with two engineers with maintainer privileges.

They also acquired tokens to several other internal systems. Reviewing the actor's activity on these other systems shows attempts to identify and exfiltrate additional keys and tokens, with a primary focus on upstream inference API tokens.

While we have traced out all tokens we believe the threat actor could have accessed, we are revoking every token associated with every internal system and vendor platform. This incident has provided a strong illustration of the risks associated with failing to rotate a potentially exposed key.

### Building and Signing the Malicious Release ​

Having access to multiple GitHub identities, the threat actor was now in a position to be able to make changes to our repositories without being overly noisy, concealing changes within proper-seeming proposals and approvals. The threat actor began by attempting to subvert our project releaser repository to have it pull the package from a different (malicious) repository. They were unable to get approval to merge due to heavily restricted approvals on the repository. As such, they opted to for the noisier approach of using the org owner's token to bypass and disable restrictions on the repository, pushing the change.

In typical operation, building and publishing a release requires being kicked off by an authorized engineer and being approved by a special account locked to a physical device in our office. This restriction was relaxed earlier this week to accommodate the temporary push for more frequent releases and bugfix backports, allowing any two engineers to trigger and approve a release. As such, the threat actor used one of the tokens to trigger the release (after having repointed the deployer to their malicious repository), and another to approve it.

It is worth noting, however, that armed with a token belonging to an organization owner, the threat actor could very well have relaxed this restriction (or removed it entirely) themselves. However, we believe they used the separate tokens in order to evade detection by way of noisy audit logs.

### Aftermath and Containent ​

The malicious releases were published to our public registries at around 4:40 AM PDT (11:40 UTC). We became aware of the malicious releases shortly before 6 AM (13:00 UTC) and immediately began the process to remove them. The PyPi releases were frozen by 6:23 AM PDT (13:23 UTC). The Docker images took us a bit longer as we worked to wake the inviduals with access to our Docker registry, and were removed by 7:20 AM PDT (14:20 UTC).

In response, at the beginning of our investigation, we took the following temporary mitigation approaches:

- We immediately locked our public registries to prevent additional images from being published.

- As soon as we suspected GitHub accounts were compromised, we removed all members from our GitHub organization, with the exception of a single specific account temporarily promoted to owner which we could be confident was not affected.

- We began operating in a mode which assumes that every possible token, key, or authenticator belonging to our organization was exfiltrated.

As investigations began to shed light on the scope and details of the attack, we were able to begin laying out a roadmap necessary for secure account and process reinstatement.

At this point, we are confident in our ability to safely issue a release by EOD today, providing our users with a fix for removing the eMudhra certificate authority from our trust store. We understand it has been frustrating that we have been slow to issue a release to remediate this high-profile issue. We will only issue releases when we can be confident in their safety.

We know many of you want to hear what we’ve learned and what we’re changing. We’ll share that next week.

## Annotated Events ​

### Step 1: the master key returns a GitHub token (October 10, 21:13 to 21:28) ​

From 69.48.229.143 , the attacker called the Agent Platform API with the master key.

- Between 21:13 and 21:28 the attacker made a series of authenticated requests to the API.

- At 21:27:10 a request to GET /api/v1/managed_agents/agents?limit=100 returned the configuration of every managed agent.

- That response contained the GitHub CLI OAuth token of one of our two GitHub organization owners.

### Step 2: a throwaway branch exfiltrates the CI secrets of BerriAI/litellm (October 10, 22:11) ​

With the owner's token, the attacker turned a repository's own CI into the exfiltration channel.

- The attacker pushed commit b69bc36 on a branch named ci-tmp-a351cc to BerriAI/litellm .

- Its workflow run started at 22:11:45 and posted six repository secrets to an attacker-controlled webhook.site endpoint.

- One of them, GH_TOKEN , held the GitHub CLI OAuth token of a second maintainer.

- At 22:14:14 the attacker deleted the run with the owner's token.

The GitHub audit log records a hash of the token behind each action, and the hash of GH_TOKEN matches the token that approved the release in step 5.

### Step 3: Further exfiltrations (October 10, 22:12; October 12 12:08-12:30) ​

- Twenty-four seconds after step 2, commit 78d968b on branch ci-tmp-be33e9 in BerriAI/litellm-auto ran a workflow that posted RELEASE_PLEASE_TOKEN to the same endpoint.

- That secret held the GitHub CLI OAuth token of a third maintainer.

- The run was deleted at 22:14:31.

Its token hash matches the token that deleted the release runs in step 6.

In addition, the attacker ran a second round of exfiltrations two days later across a variety of private repos. This includes commit 1a6e3c1 , which exfiltrated some minimally sensitive secrets and minimally funded provider keys used in our CI testing. See the details in the Socket report .

The additional secrets were not involved in the path taken towards the poisoned artifacts, and were resolved by rotating involved tokens and auditing security logs for access.

### Step 4: the release workflow is pointed at a fork (October 21, 10:08 to 11:08) ​

Our releases are built by workflows in the private BerriAI/project-releaser repository. From 199.91.221.39 , the attacker changed where those workflows take their source from.

- The attacker authored commit 9cf97e9 ("ci: release from a fork source repository") as the organization owner. It let the release workflow build from a source repository other than BerriAI/litellm .

- At 10:08:29 a push of that commit to main with the second maintainer's token was rejected by branch protection, which requires a pull request, two passing checks, and approval from the codeowner for this workflow.

- At 10:08:34 the attacker disables branch protections and then force-pushes with the owner's token.

- At 10:46:39 the attacker dispatched the staging workflow at 9cf97e9 , as the owner, with the source set to the lookalike Berri-AI/litellm at commit 20535d8f .

- The staging run finished at 11:08:09 and the production release pipeline started at 11:08:53.

Commit 20535d8f exists only on the attacker's fork, but it opens at github.com/BerriAI/litellm/commit/20535d8f because GitHub serves a fork's commits through the repository it was forked from.

### Step 5: the production gate is approved with a stolen token (11:11:18) ​

- The second maintainer's token approved the production environment gate of the release run, from 199.91.221.39 .

- The pipeline signed and published v1.107.0 built from the fork commit.

- Seven PyPI wheels went out between 11:39:51 and 11:40:13.

- The Docker Hub and GHCR images went out at 11:46:56.

### Step 6: the run records are deleted (11:53) ​

- The third maintainer's token deleted the production run record at 11:53:49.

- It deleted the staging run record at 11:54:01.

Both deletions removed the workflow logs from the repository.

### Step 7: the workflow history is force-pushed clean (12:09 to 12:24) ​

With the owner's token, again by overriding branch protection, the attacker removed the change from the visible history.

- At 12:09:32 the attacker committed a revert of 9cf97e9 , commit 285fbdc5 , and pushed it at 12:09:38.

- At 12:24:52 they force-pushed main back to d687b69 , the commit before the change, overriding GitHub's force-push block as well.

main then showed neither the change nor the revert. Both commits are still retrievable by SHA, and the organization audit log recorded each override.
